text: We saw how a community in a graph can evolve. To track the nature of evolution, we need
to measure how the community changes over time. So here are three cases, one, two, and
three, of a community changing between two observation points. The goal is to figure
out whether these are normal fluctuations in the network or a more drastic change is
occurring. Look at them for a second. Just visually, the first case seems to show just
minor changes, whereas case 2 shows a merger and case 3 shows a split. Now, to come up
with a quantitative measure of change over time, we need to take two observations from
two consecutive time points and fuse the graph.
If you do it for case one, you will find one new node, one leaving node, and the rest
are common over time.
For case two, you will see that two previous communities colored differently are internally
connected the same way as before, but some members of the two communities have created
new cross-links.
3? Well, I see one joint node, colored purple. Apart from it, there are just two edges connecting
the two groups. Now, with these observations, we can now compute the autocorrelation between
the graphs across time t and t plus 1. This is just a measure of the number of common
nodes divided by the number of nodes in the combined graph.
If a community does not change at all, this number is 1.
If a community has only a few connections, the number is lower.
After computing autocorrelation over every pair of time steps, we can then compute stationarity,
which measures the overall change in the autocorrelation over a period of time.
So if we measure over 100 timesteps, we will add the 99 correlation values from the steps
and then divide it by 99.
This will tell us what fraction of members remain unchanged on an average over these
100 timestamps.
Therefore the 1 minus zeta tells us the average ratio of members that have changed in a timestep.
Let's take three cases.
In the first plot, the size of the graph is small, and nothing much is happening here.
A node occasionally joins or leaves, keeping the stationarity pretty flat.
In the second case, the graph is small, but there are a lot of changes, especially at
time step 7.
A whole bunch of purple nodes have joined, and then they went away.
The size of the graph clearly reflects this with a purple spike that you see on the size
versus the time graph.
This spike on the time series, by the way, is called a burst.
The third plot shows a large graph with many nodes joining and leaving.
The stationarity of this graph will be quite low given the abrupt changes we observe over
time.
